raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department in December 2016 with new-onset tonic-clonic seizures, on a background of 19 kg weight loss, progressive lethargy and cognitive decline over the preceding 18 months. He had travelled extensively across the African subcontinent whilst working aboard a ship and during this time had engaged in unprotected intercourse with female sex workers.
Salient examination findings included nystagmus on right-lateral gaze, past-pointing in the left upper limb, brisk reflexes and an unsteady gait, suggestive of underlying cerebellar pathology. Following biochemical and serological investigations, the patient was diagnosed with HIV-1, with a viral load of 1 243 938 copies/mL and a CD4 lymphocyte count of 12 cells/microL. Initial computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed multiple lesions in the brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia and both cerebral hemispheres, with significant local mass effect and effacement of the left lateral ventricle. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was also undertaken at this time, which demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions (Figure 1). Mediastinal and hilar lymph node enlargement identified on CT imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis was felt to be in keeping with persistent generalised lymphadenopathy (PGL) because of advanced HIV as there was no palpable cervical, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy (Figure 2).
The patient was commenced on treatment for presumptive toxoplasmosis, with sulfadiazine/pyramethamine/folinic acid and adjunctive high-dose dexamethasone, levetiracetam. He also simultaneously commenced antiretroviral therapy (ART) comprising of tenofovir/emtricitabine and dolutegravir, along with prophylactic antibiotics and antifungals against opportunistic infections. Blood cultures were negative as was toxoplasma serum Immunoglobulin G (IgG). Tuberculosis with CNS involvement and cryptococcoma were considered as differential diagnoses; however, cryptococcal antigen was negative as subsequently were mycobacterial blood and induced sputum cultures. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was not attempted in light of the cerebellar lesions.
Following 2 weeks of toxoplasmosis treatment, there was no improvement in the appearances of the intra-cranial lesions on repeat MR brain imaging, with two new lesions being identified (Figure 3). At this point, alternative diagnoses such as systemic lymphoma with intra-cranial metastases and PCNSL were pursued over toxoplasmosis. A fluodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography (FDG-PET-CT) and brain biopsy were, thus, arranged with the aim of obtaining a more definitive diagnosis.
FDG-PET-CT was undertaken 3 weeks following initial presentation and demonstrated high avidity activity only in the brain including the right parietal, right parieto-occipital and left frontal regions as well as the cerebellum and basal ganglia (standardised uptake value [SUV] max 7.3 compared with normal brain cortex). No FDG-avid mediastinal lymph nodes were identified and these appearances pointed towards the diagnosis of PCNSL, rather than systemic lymphoma with cerebral metastases.
The right parietal lobe brain biopsy demonstrated a suspicious lymphoid infiltrate. Mycobacterial and fungal stains were negative as was immunostaining for herpes simplex virus (HSV1), HSV2, cytomegalovirus (CMV) and John Cunningham virus (JCV). Epstein-Barr encoding region (EBER) in situ hybridisation staining was also negative; however, this was a likely false negative result, in the context of necrosis and ribonucleic acid (RNA) degradation. Within the necrotic areas, the cellular outlines and remains were strongly positive for CD20, CD79a and BCL2. They were negative for CD19, CD3, CD5, CD10, BCL6 and PAX5. Final histopathology results were in keeping with a high-grade B-cell lymphoma that was necrotic.
The patient was commenced on MATRix chemotherapy (rituximab, methotrexate, cytarabine, with omission of thioTEPA for the first two cycles) for HIV-associated primary cerebral lymphoma. Within 8 weeks of commencement of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), there was a 3log10 fold decrease in HIV-1 viral load. There has also been a marked improvement in cognitive function and gait following four cycles of MATRix chemotherapy (Figure 4).
Repeat MRI imaging 6 months following initial presentation also demonstrates a reduction in volume of the supra and infra-tentorial parenchymal and sub-ependymal lesions, with improvement in the degree of peri-lesional vasogenic oedema, in keeping with a positive disease response (Figure 5). The patient continues to make good progress and is currently being worked up for consolidative therapy with an autologous stem cell transplantation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department in December 2016 with new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures superimposed on an 18-month history of 19 kg weight loss, progressive lethargy, and cognitive decline.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 18 months preceding presentation, the patient experienced an unintentional 19 kg weight loss, progressive lethargy, and cognitive deterioration, culminating in acute generalized tonic-clonic seizures in December 2016.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy merchant seaman; epidemiological history notable for extensive travel across the African subcontinent while working aboard a ship and unprotected sexual intercourse with female commercial sex workers.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for new-onset tonic-clonic seizures, 19 kg weight loss, lethargy, cognitive decline, and gait unsteadiness.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination revealed right-lateral gaze-evoked nystagmus, left upper limb dysmetria (past-pointing), generalized hyperreflexia, cognitive impairment, and an ataxic gait, without palpable cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood cultures, mycobacterial blood and induced sputum cultures, serum Toxoplasma IgG, and serum cryptococcal antigen were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 12 cells/µL. Head CT and contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions across the brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and bilateral cerebral hemispheres with local mass effect and left lateral ventricular effacement (growing with 2 new lesions after 2 weeks of empiric anti-toxoplasmosis therapy). Chest/abdomen/pelvis CT showed mild mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy consistent with HIV persistent generalized lymphadenopathy. Whole-body FDG-PET/CT at week 3 showed intense hypermetabolic uptake confined exclusively to the brain lesions (right parietal, right parieto-occipital, left frontal, cerebellum, and basal ganglia; SUVmax 7.3) with no FDG-avid systemic lymphadenopathy. Right parietal lobe brain biopsy confirmed necrotic high-grade B-cell primary CNS lymphoma (tumor cells strongly positive for CD20, CD79a, and BCL2; negative for CD3, CD5, CD10, BCL6, HSV-1/2, CMV, JCV, and fungal/mycobacterial stains).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Multifocal supra- and infratentorial HIV-associated primary central nervous system high-grade B-cell lymphoma (PCNSL: CD20+, CD79a+, BCL2+) unmasking newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection (baseline plasma HIV-1 viral load 1,243,938 copies/mL, CD4+ count 12 cells/µL). After failing 2 weeks of empiric sulfadiazine/pyrimethamine/folinic acid and high-dose dexamethasone for initially suspected cerebral toxoplasmosis (with negative Toxo IgG), FDG-PET/CT and right parietal brain biopsy established PCNSL. Treatment with 4 cycles of MATRix immunochemotherapy (rituximab, high-dose methotrexate, and cytarabine, omitting thiotepa in cycles 1–2) alongside concurrent HAART (tenofovir/emtricitabine and dolutegravir) and levetiracetam achieved a 3-log10 reduction in HIV-1 viral load within 8 weeks, marked recovery of cognition and gait, and substantial supra-/infratentorial tumor regression on 6-month brain MRI prior to planned consolidative autologous stem cell transplantation.
